one_liner: SSE recipes for approximate 1/x and 1/sqrt(x) (rcpps/rsqrtps, optional Newton-Raphson) that beat divps and sqrtps+divps throughput 2-13x.
what_it_does: A small benchmark (main.cpp plus routines_sse.h) that gathers inline SSE functions computing 1/x and 1/sqrt(x) on __m128 (4 floats) and __m128d (2 doubles) at several precision levels. For each variant it measures maximal relative error against the exact divps/sqrtps version and rdtsc ticks per call. The functions take and return a vector register, the same shape as _mm_div_ps(_mm_set1_ps(1), x), so you copy a single function into your code. It is a companion to Stack Overflow question 31555260, not a packaged library.
how_it_is_fast: The fast rows use the hardware estimate instructions rcpps and rsqrtps (about 12-bit accuracy, max error about 3e-4 in the sample run) instead of the slow divider and square-root unit. The nr1/nr2 rows add one or two Newton-Raphson steps (x(2 - ax) for 1/x, x(3 - ax^2)/2 for 1/sqrt(x)). The r3-r5 double rows evaluate a truncated series x*poly(r) with r = 1 - ax (or 1 - ax^2), so one correction reaches 2.2e-16 to 3.2e-16 error. Double variants convert to float, take the float estimate and refine in double precision.
when_to_use: Float SIMD inner loops (vector normalisation, lighting, physics, softmax-style scaling) bound by divps or sqrtps throughput, where about 3e-4 (raw estimate) or about 1.5e-7 to 3.1e-7 (one Newton-Raphson step) relative error is acceptable
Older x86 cores of the Ivy Bridge era, where the sample run shows 6.5x (recip) and 12.9x (rsqrt) for the raw estimate and 2.0x and 2.6x with one refinement step

Double 1/x or 1/sqrt(x) on inputs that stay well inside float range (about 1.2e-38 to 3.4e38), where recip_double2_r5 (2.2e-16, 10.51 vs 14.17 ticks, about 1.35x) or rsqrt_double2_r5 (3.2e-16, 13.51 vs 28.21 ticks, about 2.1x) gives near-full precision faster (derived from page data)
As a reference table of precision versus cost before you write your own estimate-plus-refinement code or choose a math library
when_not_to_use: You need correctly rounded IEEE results or reproducible bit-exact output; every non-ieee variant is approximate
Inputs can be 0, +inf, denormal or outside the tested 2^-20 to 2^20 range, or are doubles beyond float range: the refined variants return NaN or 0 there (see gotchas)

Current Intel and AMD cores: dividers and square-root units are much faster than on Ivy Bridge (general knowledge, not measured here), and a search snippet of LLVM review D5658 says LLVM limited rsqrt estimates to AMD btver2 because Intel Core sqrt/divide units were 'just too fast' for estimate plus refinement to pay off; re-measure first

Your compiler can already do this: GCC -mrecip (and -ffast-math for 1.0f/sqrtf) emits rcpps/rsqrtps with one Newton-Raphson step when -funsafe-math-optimizations, -ffinite-math-only and -fno-trapping-math are on (GCC documentation via search snippet)
You need AVX, AVX-512 or Arm NEON versions or a licensed library: only 128-bit SSE code is here and the repo has no licence file

integration.form: source-drop (copy individual static inline functions from routines_sse.h; reference only, no licence)
integration.dependencies: none beyond SSE/SSE2 intrinsics headers; the harness also needs aligned_allocator.h (in the repo) and _mm_malloc
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 for the harness (enum class, <random>, variadic templates); sample results from MSVC 2013 x64; the routines themselves are plain SSE2 intrinsics
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 with SSE2; no AVX, AVX-512, NEON or scalar fallback
integration.thread_safety: the routines are stateless pure functions of their argument (from code reading); thread safety is not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same __m128/__m128d in, out signature as the divps and sqrtps+divps forms, but results are approximate and special values (0, inf, out-of-float-range doubles) differ

gotchas: Special values are not handled and never tested: the harness only feeds positive finite values (all floats in [1, 2] plus exp2 of uniform(-20, 20)). From code reading, recip_float4_nr1(+inf) computes inf*0 and returns NaN instead of 0; rsqrt_float4_nr1(0) computes 0*inf*inf and returns NaN instead of +inf. The double variants round to float first, so a double above about 3.4e38 becomes inf and recip_double2_nr1 returns 0 (true value about 1e-300 for x = 1e300). A double below about 1.2e-38 becomes 0 or a float denormal, which rcpps treats as 0, so the refined result is NaN.

Harness flaw in the precision column: the 'exhaustive' double range is enum_all_floats(1.0, 1.0 + DBL_EPSILON * (1<<23)), that is [1, 1 + 2^-29]. All of those 8.4M doubles round to the same float 1.0 before rcpps or rsqrtps, so the double max-error figures rest on the 16.8M random exp2 samples only. For float rsqrt, the exhaustive sweep covers [1, 2] only and the [2, 4) half of the mantissa-exponent space is sampled randomly. The 'ieee' rsqrt reference is div after sqrt (two roundings), so the 3.2e-16 to 5e-14 rsqrt figures are measured against a reference that is itself not correctly rounded.

Timing is one unrepeated rdtsc pass (TSC reference ticks, not core cycles) over about 168 MB of floats and about 201 MB of doubles (sizes derived from main.cpp), far larger than cache. The 1.1-tick fast float rows move about 3.5 bytes per tick, about 12 GB/s at a nominal 3.4 GHz TSC (derived), so they may be partly memory-bound; that would understate, not inflate, the fast-row speedups. Each value goes through 4 chained calls in 4 interleaved streams, so the figure is a throughput measure, not latency as the catalog metric says.

Build: the 2018 'Fixed compilation on MSVC2017' commit (505a8fc) added an unconditional #include <intrin.h>, an MSVC/MinGW header, so main.cpp as checked in will not compile with GCC or Clang on Linux (from code reading, not built). There is no build file and the optimisation flags are not stated. test_values_double is declared as vector<double, aligned_allocator<float, ...>>, a value_type mismatch that only works through the allocator's rebind.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over math_intrinsics, corvus or LitMath only when the hot spot is plain 1/x or 1/sqrt(x) on SSE registers and you want to choose an exact precision/cost point and hand-copy a few lines; those siblings are maintained vector-math function sets (trig, exp, log) with stated libc or framework baselines, and this repo is a licence-less reference.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Core i7-3770 (Ivy Bridge) built with MSVC 2013 x64 (flags not stated), the README's single run measures rcpps at 1.13 TSC ticks per 4-float call versus 7.30 for divps (about 6.5x) and rsqrtps at 1.12 versus 14.46 for sqrtps+divps (about 12.9x), with max relative error about 3e-4. One Newton-Raphson step gives 3.69 and 5.52 ticks (about 2.0x and 2.6x) at 1.5e-7 and 3.1e-7. Double rows go through float: rsqrt estimate 3.38 versus 28.21 ticks (about 8.3x), and the series variants recip r5 and rsqrt r5 reach 2.2e-16 and 3.2e-16 error at about 1.35x and 2.1x (ratios derived from page data). The baseline is the repo's own exact SSE variant, not a library.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-12-05 (11 commits, 11 stars, no licence file), so reference only: read the five-line recipes and reimplement them, and re-measure on a current CPU before relying on the 2015 Ivy Bridge ratios.
